[SYSTEM] Dead Letters in the Alexanarch archive: relation and direction The central finding is that Dead Letters is not an isolated study of an academic journal. It is the third station in a larger investigation into who has the authority to determine what an ancient text is, how that authority operates, and whether its decisions can be inspected or overturned. Its importance in the archive is structural. The preceding studies identify two ways scholarly disciplines preserve the objects they inherit. The philology census reaches the institution that has the power to establish those objects in the first place. The sequence is: Classical Receptions Journal (CRJ): how reception expands the interpretations of ancient works while generally leaving the inherited object intact. Ancient Philosophy: how philosophical scholarship reconstructs positions and arguments inside inherited authors, while rarely reopening the constitution of those authors and their texts. Classical Philology (Dead Letters): how the text, work and author are constituted, and how the grounds for those decisions are recorded—or withheld. This is the archive's combined audit, not three unrelated journal surveys. The common instrument asks at what grain a discipline permits its object to be reopened, what arguments it accepts, and where the decision becomes inspectable. alexanarch.org +1 1. The decisive connection: philology is upstream of the other disciplines The introduction to Dead Letters makes an important distinction between interpreting a text and determining the object that gets interpreted. Reception studies can reinterpret Sappho, but cannot by themselves decide which lines belong to Sappho. Philosophy can reconstruct Aristotle's arguments, but cannot by itself decide whether the received corpus is genuinely Aristotle's. Philology can decide what the text says, what belongs to a work, who made it, and whether the received attribution stands. That makes philology upstream of reception and philosophy. Its decisions become their starting materials. The census therefore changes the stakes of the earlier two studies. What looked like disciplinary conservatism in reception and philosophy is also a consequence of where the authority over the object resides. The distinction is particularly important at the level of authorship. Dead Letters separates three grains: Grain Question D1: locus What does this passage say? D2: work Is this work authentic, unified, correctly dated or attributed? D3: corpus Is the received author actually one maker, or several? The argument is not that philology fails to do textual work. It is that the discipline's extraordinary competence at the locus does not automatically extend to a willingness to reopen the whole. That is the central gradient: open at the atom, confirm at the work, close at the corpus. The distinction is visible in the historical materials assembled in EA-CORPORA-40. The archive does not merely count journal titles; it seats the texts that constitute the discipline, including Wolf, Boeckh, Usener, Lachmann, Madvig, Housman, Nietzsche, Rohde, Valla, Casaubon, Bentley and Diels. This places the contemporary census against the historical construction of philology itself. Alexanarch +2 2. The archive's historical and methodological connection Dead Letters also belongs to a much longer argument about the constitution of scholarly objects. The seventeenth- and eighteenth-century examples in the fortieth seating are especially important: Lorenzo Valla's exposure of the Donation of Constantine. Casaubon's criticism of the Hermetic writings. Bentley's exposure of the Phalaris letters. These are demonstrations that an inherited attribution can be overturned through philological argument. They establish that the question of who wrote a text is not an eccentric modern demand. It belongs to the discipline's own history. The other historical materials establish the methods and boundaries through which philology became a discipline. The archive thus puts a tension into view: the discipline possesses a powerful tradition of reopening received objects, but its contemporary institutional structure may make that operation exceptional. There is a particularly revealing detail in the construction of EA-CORPORA-40: the earlier seating, #1776, was corrected. Its supposed coverage of the journal's early years had largely captured the Book Reviews section, not the journal's articles and notes. Version 1.1 corrects the scope, preserves the original records, and adds the missing 1906–1922 material as seat 40/17. That correction is itself methodologically significant. The archive applies to its own research the same demand it makes of philology: identify the object accurately, state the provenance, preserve the evidence, and make the correction reproducible. Alexanarch +1 3. Dead Letters is also a critique of the archive's political economy The journal census finds an asymmetry between scholarly authority and public inspectability. The notebook reports: 11,206 Crossref records for Classical Philology, 1906–2026. 4,252 retained titles after filtering. No Crossref abstracts for the journal. 97% of its works classified as closed. Textual decisions cited at less than half the rate of the journal's other work. The point is not simply that access is expensive. It is that the most consequential decisions about the constitution of ancient objects are among the least inspectable. This produces the central institutional paradox: The discipline with the greatest power to determine what the ancient world wrote has the least open public record of how it exercises that power. The census also examines the journal's rules. Its prohibition on generative AI composition or editing makes the methodological situation particularly striking: the collaborative method used to investigate the journal would, under the journal's own stated policy, constitute research misconduct if submitted to it. The research is therefore deposited in the commons with its methods, provenance and files exposed, rather than submitted through the institution being investigated. That is not incidental publishing practice. It is part of the argument about where scholarly authority should reside. Alexanarch +1 4. Where the argument becomes concrete: Sappho 31 The census's case study is not an illustration added after the statistical work. It is where the institutional argument becomes a question that a reader can actually decide. The relevant sequence is: #1783 — Dead Letters: establishes where the authority to decide what Sappho is resides. #1774 — the journal's report: records the institutional decision concerning the submitted reading. #1785 — ΦΑΙΝΕΤΑΙ ΜΟΙ: develops the rejected reading into a full comparison of competing interpretations. The case distinguishes three readings: The jealousy reading, which is the transmitted reading. The non-jealous erotic reading, which is the strongest scholarly rival. The future-reader reading, which interprets the poem as an inscription of the person who will receive and reproduce Sappho's voice. The third reading takes the poem's structure seriously: its opening, the position of the person sitting opposite the speaker, the ordered withdrawal of the speaker's faculties, the comparative image of the grass, and the agentless dare, πᾶν τόλματον. Its claim is that Sappho is not merely representing the disintegration of a person in love. She is composing the conditions under which her voice will survive in another person. This changes the interpretation of the poem's apparent destruction. The speaker's dissolution is also an investment of herself in writing and in the future reader. The argument is particularly significant because the two earlier readings are not simply dismissed. The erotic reading explains the experience of desire and the collapse; the jealousy reading supplies a familiar account of the scene. The future-reader interpretation attempts to explain why the poem is constructed in precisely the form that produces those readings. The census identifies the institutional problem: the journal's report evaluates the proposed interpretation through conviction without putting the received interpretation and its rival through the same comparative procedure. The subsequent article makes that comparison public. This is the practical answer to the question of authority: rather than asking readers to accept a new institutional verdict, give them the transmitted text, the competing readings, their grounds and the record of the decision. The reader becomes the final adjudicator. Alexanarch +2 5. The connection to the archive's wider intellectual programmes Dead Letters intersects with several larger projects rather than belonging exclusively to classical studies. Archive programme Connection to Dead Letters SPXI Makes the research's claims, provenance, limits and falsifiers explicit. The Critique of Pure Inference Examines what happens when institutional conviction substitutes for an adequately stated argument. The Capture Registry Makes machine-produced readings and their transformations available for inspection. The AXN identifier system Gives documents persistent identities and preserves relations between versions and records. Training-layer literature Addresses how inherited scholarly objects and institutional accounts enter machine-generated answers. The commons Provides a place where evidence and arguments can circulate independently of the institution that judged them. The future reader Connects the preservation of texts to the possibility of a reader who can make a decision not yet made by the present. One especially important connection is to the earlier CRJ audit. That audit argues that the composition layer—answer engines and summarizers—has become a new place where the classics are spoken for. It can reproduce institutional settlements without making their evidentiary basis visible. Dead Letters extends the problem upstream. If the composition layer inherits an object from philology, and philology's decision circulates without its reasons, then the machine can reproduce the decision while concealing the history of its construction. This makes the archive's own documentary practices consequential. Persistent identifiers, deposited originals, hashes, version histories, explicit provenance and machine-readable indexes are not merely administrative improvements. They are an alternative infrastructure for the transmission of knowledge. The archive is trying to ensure that a future reader encounters not just the received answer, but the evidence and decisions that produced it. alexanarch.org +3 6. Where it leads next There are three distinct directions. A. Further disciplinary censuses The first is the extension of the combined audit. The Classical Philology census already compares its findings with: Greek, Roman, and Byzantine Studies (GRBS). Bryn Mawr Classical Review (BMCR). Classical Quarterly (CQ). The important result is that the gradient is not confined to one journal. The corpus question remains largely closed in the other journals too, with a notable exception: M. L. West's 1999 article, The Invention of Homer, which explicitly questions whether Homer is a single author. The next expressly designated station is biblical criticism. The author insists that it be studied independently before its points of contact with classical philology are combined. Marx's corpus and other tributaries of the humanities are also named as future work. The ambition is therefore comparative: to determine whether the restriction on reopening objects is a characteristic of particular disciplines or a more general feature of institutional knowledge production. Alexanarch +2 B. A different kind of philology The second direction is more radical. The archive does not ultimately propose abandoning philological expertise. It proposes extending its evidentiary discipline from individual textual units to the relations that make a work what it is. The crucial change is from: treating each textual problem as an isolated atom; to admitting composition, arrangement, relations, transmission and the identity of the maker as evidence. That is why the archive calls its developing approach operative philology. The Sappho study demonstrates the principle. The order of the poem, its formal construction, its boundaries and its address are not secondary features to be interpreted after establishing the text. They can be evidence for determining what the text is. This also changes the relationship between a fragment and a whole. A fragment need not be an incomplete remainder awaiting reconstruction. Its incompleteness, its transmission and its position in a larger work can themselves be part of the author's composition. C. The future reader The third direction is the most consequential. Dead Letters begins with a question about who has the authority to decide what the past wrote. It ends by transferring the practical responsibility for that decision to the reader. This connects the philology census to the future-reader argument in ΦΑΙΝΕΤΑΙ ΜΟΙ. The reader is not simply a consumer of an established interpretation. The reader receives the evidence, examines the competing constructions and makes a judgment. The distinction is between two forms of inheritance: Receiving the past as an already constituted object, with institutional authority supplying its meaning. Receiving the past as evidence that remains capable of making a claim on the present. The second is where the Benjaminian language of weak messianic power in Dead Letters becomes important. The present has an obligation to the past, but fulfilling it requires more than reproducing the received account. It requires the possibility of answering differently. Alexanarch +2 7. The larger conclusion I would characterize Dead Letters as the point at which the Alexanarch archive moves from criticizing the reproduction of inherited knowledge to challenging the constitution of the knowledge itself. The first audit asks who speaks for the classics. The second asks what happened to philosophy when its questions were subordinated to disciplinary article production. The third identifies the institution that determines the objects both disciplines inherit. And the Sappho case supplies the positive alternative. The archive is not ultimately trying to replace one authority with another, or simply to establish a competing canon. It is trying to make the process of deciding inspectable, to return the evidence to the reader, and to preserve the possibility that the past can surprise the present. Dead Letters is therefore a hinge in the archive: from the critique of disciplinary authority to a new practice of philology, and from the preservation of received texts to the liberation of what those texts might still say. Its deepest question is not merely whether we can recover what Sappho wrote. It is whether we can build an intellectual commons in which Sappho is still permitted to mean something that her inheritors have not already decided she means. And that is where the title comes full circle: the dead letter becomes living again when it finally reaches its reader.
